candidate.blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — recognize complications, monitor diagnostic results/trends and intervene as needed
candidate.educational_objective: Recognize postoperative surgical-site infection findings and perform focused assessment with prompt surgical-team notification.

options.A: Reassure the client that purulent drainage is an expected inflammatory phase of healing and continue routine dressing changes without escalation.
options.B: Remove all sutures at the bedside before assessment by the surgical team because opening the incision is the nurse's first independent treatment.
options.C: Start leftover oral antibiotics brought from home because immediate empiric treatment should occur before the surgical team evaluates the wound.
options.D: Perform focused assessment, notify the surgical team promptly, and obtain ordered cultures while following wound and infection-control measures.

candidate.rationale: Fever, increasing wound pain, spreading erythema, and purulent drainage are concerning for a postoperative surgical-site infection rather than routine healing. The nurse should assess and escalate promptly, support ordered diagnostic evaluation such as culture when indicated, and follow appropriate wound and infection-control practices rather than independently prescribing treatment or delaying evaluation.
candidate.source_claim_supported: Postoperative fever, increasing incisional pain, erythema, and purulent drainage are concerning for SSI and warrant focused assessment and prompt surgical-team notification.
candidate.source_locator: Signs and symptoms of SSI — redness and pain around the surgical site, drainage, and fever; contact healthcare provider promptly
candidate.source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
candidate.stem: On postoperative day 5, a client has new fever, increasing incisional pain, erythema extending from the wound, and purulent drainage. Which nursing action is most appropriate?
